title: Crosscurrents
scene: An old way of helping no longer fits.

paragraphs: She touched the floor beside her.
Mukund moved a roll of masking tape and lowered himself. His knee clicked. She put her hand over his.
"I was going to stand by this one," she said. "At the opening. Just at the beginning."
"I'd even worked out where to put my bag."

Before a group show a year and a half ago, a frame had split in a taxi. Mukund had asked the driver to stop beside a hardware store. He returned with glue, two clamps and tape that left silver patches on both their sleeves.

They held the corners together on the sidewalk. He had missed his own dinner reservation while she waited for the glue to set. At the gallery she squeezed his hand and told him she could not have managed without him.
She looked at his hand now, open on his knee.
Her phone played the beginning of a voice message before she could silence it. The shop bell in New Jersey, then her father saying, "We put it up. Your mother says the blue looks..."
He nodded. She wished she had said it less sharply, but he was already looking at the table.
He knew the next morning would be harder if he left it. He also knew that saying so would sound like something he wanted her to be grateful for.
She nodded. He went to the kitchen.
The call was about the appointment he had left unfinished. No, the hospital had not withdrawn. He would send the revised figures before nine. Yes, tomorrow morning.

He stood beside the sink after the call ended. In their second year together, he had missed a quarterly target and told Aarna he was fine. She ordered dinner and talked about a film. He remembered being relieved.
Had she known he was upset? He had never asked.
When he returned, she was stacking the invitations.
He reached for the laptop. She moved the last invitation from beneath its corner.
He carried the cups to the sink. One was almost full. Tea had dried in a brown line inside the other.
He washed both, then found himself washing one again.
At six, the light had left the square of paper on the wall.
Aarna opened her father's photograph again. In the shop window the invitation was no larger than the guitar's sound hole. Anyone walking past would have to stop to read it.
She typed, "Can I call you tomorrow?"
The reply arrived while she was still holding the phone. "Of course."
Mukund brought her a glass of water.
He sat in the chair this time.
"You have to stay strong, Aarna. Don't let one afternoon..."
She turned Room Enough towards the wall.
"I don't want to look at it."
He reached for the frame. She caught it first. For a second they held opposite sides.
